summary: An antipsychotic used for schizophrenia and bipolar depression. Taken once daily with a real meal (at least 350 calories) so your body absorbs it. It has a lower risk of weight and blood-sugar problems than many antipsychotics, but watch for a strong inner restlessness (akathisia), stiffness or shaking, sleepiness and rare serious reactions such as a rare emergency with very high fever, rigid muscles and confusion.
description: Latuda (lurasidone) is a second-generation antipsychotic used to treat schizophrenia and depressive episodes in bipolar I disorder. It can start helping within 1–2 weeks, with more noticeable improvement over 4–6 weeks. The most important thing to know is absorption: you need to take it with at least 350 calories, or your body may absorb much less of the dose. Compared with many antipsychotics, it is usually easier on weight and cholesterol, but it can still cause akathisia (inner restlessness), stiffness or shaking (parkinsonism), nausea and sleep changes. It is not approved for dementia-related psychosis because antipsychotics raised the risk of death in that group.
patient_summary: Latuda is used for schizophrenia and bipolar depression. Take it once daily with food (≥350 calories) or it may not work as intended. Some people feel less depression or clearer thinking within 1–2 weeks, with fuller benefit by 4–6 weeks. Common issues are restlessness (akathisia), stiffness/shakiness (parkinsonism), nausea, and sleep disruption or sleepiness. Compared with many antipsychotics it tends to be lighter on weight and cholesterol, but metabolic monitoring still matters. It’s not approved for dementia-related psychosis because antipsychotics raise the risk of death in that group.

primary.context: Lurasidone is an FDA-approved option for schizophrenia in adults and adolescents. Improvement may begin within 1–2 weeks, with continued gains through 4–6 weeks.
FDA-approved for depressive episodes in bipolar I disorder, either on its own or (in adults) as an add-on to lithium or divalproex. It does not work for acute bipolar mania or hypomania.

off_label.context: Sometimes used for depressive episodes that also have some manic symptoms (mixed features) in bipolar disorder or major depressive disorder. This is off-label and should be guided by a specialist.
Used off-label for postpartum psychosis in some treatment plans, with the dose raised step by step to a higher level and a set treatment period (months), under specialist psychiatric care.

therapeutic_response.display: Schizophrenia: initial effects often within 1–2 weeks; Bipolar depression: initial effects often within 1 week with continued improvement through ~6 weeks

common_adverse_effects.incidence: Adults: ~6% to 22% reported; adolescents also reported
common_adverse_effects.notes: This can feel like anxiety, but it’s more physical—an internal motor that won’t shut off. It often appears early or after dose increases. If you’re pacing, can’t sit through a movie, or feel ‘crawly’ in your body, tell your prescriber quickly—this is treatable and sometimes a reason to raise the dose more slowly or switch.

common_adverse_effects.effect: Stiffness, shaking or slowness (movement side effects, parkinsonism)
common_adverse_effects.incidence: Adults: EPS reported up to ~5% to 39%; parkinsonism ~5% to 17%
common_adverse_effects.notes: Stiffness, tremor, slowed movement, jaw tightness, or swallowing changes can happen. These side effects are dose-related and may show up days to weeks after starting or increasing the dose.

Latuda is often described as mildly to moderately sedating compared with other antipsychotics. Some people feel sleepy at night (helpful), others feel foggy. Sedation often improves over time, but if it’s flattening you, the dose or timing may need adjustment.

Yes, both can happen: some people get sleepy, others feel wired. If sleep gets worse, it may be related to the dose or timing, or it may actually be inner restlessness (akathisia) that looks like ‘insomnia.’
Taking it with food helps tolerability and absorption. If nausea shows up early, it often settles, but persistent nausea matters—don’t just suffer through it silently.

common_adverse_effects.incidence: Weight gain reported ~2% to 7%; lipid/glucose changes reported in labeling
common_adverse_effects.notes: Latuda is usually more metabolically friendly than many antipsychotics, and some people even improve labs when switching from higher-risk meds. Still: monitor weight, glucose/A1C, and lipids because risk isn’t zero.

common_adverse_effects.incidence: Dose-dependent; elevated prolactin reported (higher thresholds noted in labeling tables)
common_adverse_effects.notes: If you notice sexual side effects, menstrual changes, breast tenderness or discharge, acne/hirsutism changes, or fertility issues, bring it up. Sometimes the fix is dose, switching, or choosing a more prolactin-sparing option.

serious_risks.risk: A rare emergency with fever, severe muscle stiffness, confusion and unstable heart rate, blood pressure and sweating (neuroleptic malignant syndrome, NMS). This is a medical emergency.
Tardive dyskinesia — involuntary movements of the face, tongue or limbs that can last. The risk increases with longer use and older age.
Severe dizziness or fainting when standing up (a drop in blood pressure), and falls: injury risk, especially in older adults or with dehydration.
Blood count problems: low white blood cells, low platelets or anemia. A blood count (CBC) should be checked if you have had low counts before or have signs of infection.
Hyperglycemia/diabetes: uncommon compared with some SGAs but possible; monitor labs and symptoms (thirst, urination, fatigue).

Heart-rhythm changes (QT prolongation, seen on an ECG): the overall effect is small compared with many antipsychotics, but QT prolongation has been reported after approval, so extra care is needed if you have heart risk factors or take interacting medicines.
Temperature dysregulation/heat stroke risk: especially during heat exposure, dehydration, strenuous exercise.
Suicidal ideation reported postmarketing: monitor mood and safety, especially during early treatment or changes.

safety.black_box_warning: Older adults with dementia-related psychosis who are treated with antipsychotic medicines have a higher risk of death. Lurasidone is not approved for treating dementia-related psychosis.

contraindications.contraindication: Hypersensitivity to lurasidone or any component (including angioedema history with lurasidone)
Taking it with medicines that strongly slow how it is broken down (eg, ketoconazole, clarithromycin, ritonavir, voriconazole, mibefradil)
Taking it with medicines that strongly speed up how it is broken down (eg, rifampin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, St. John's wort, avasimibe)

precautions: Suicidal thoughts and behaviors: In short-term studies, antidepressants raised this risk in children, teenagers and young adults. Watch for worsening mood or new suicidal thoughts and tell your prescriber right away (this warning is usually included when the medicine is used for mood).
A rare but life-threatening emergency with fever, stiffness, confusion and unstable heart rate and blood pressure (neuroleptic malignant syndrome, NMS)
Tardive dyskinesia — involuntary movements that can last: the risk rises with time and total amount taken
Metabolic changes: weight, glucose, and lipids can change even if risk is lower than some other antipsychotics
Dizziness or fainting when standing up (a drop in blood pressure), and falls: especially early on, with dose changes, or in older adults
Seizure risk: extra caution if you have had seizures or are more prone to them
Temperature dysregulation: higher risk during heat exposure, dehydration, strenuous exercise

interactions.interactant: Medicines that strongly slow how lurasidone is broken down (eg, ketoconazole, clarithromycin, ritonavir, voriconazole, mibefradil)
interactions.mechanism: Lurasidone levels rise sharply, raising the risk of movement side effects, sleepiness, low blood pressure and other toxic effects.
interactions.action: Should not be used together. A different antipsychotic, or a different infection or antiviral medicine, should be chosen.

interactions.interactant: Medicines that strongly speed up how lurasidone is broken down (eg, rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St. John's wort, avasimibe)
interactions.mechanism: Lurasidone levels drop sharply, so it may stop working and symptoms may return.
interactions.action: Should not be used together. Use a different medicine instead.

interactions.mechanism: Can increase serum concentrations (CYP3A4 interaction) → more side effects
interactions.action: Avoid grapefruit products while taking Latuda.

interactions.interactant: Other CNS-active meds that worsen movement side effects (certain antidepressants, stimulants, other antipsychotics)
interactions.mechanism: Higher risk of inner restlessness, stiffness or shaking, because the effects on dopamine add up.
interactions.action: Use caution with polypharmacy; monitor EPS closely during changes.

interactions.interactant: Blood pressure-lowering meds or dehydration states
interactions.mechanism: Higher risk of dizziness or fainting when standing up (a drop in blood pressure).
interactions.action: Drink enough fluids, change position slowly, and get close follow-up when starting or raising doses.

monitoring_requirements.parameter: Adherence and dosing-with-food check at every visit: confirm ≥350 calories each dose and consistent timing
Mental status and target symptoms every visit: mood, psychosis intensity, agitation, sleep, functioning

Inner restlessness and other movement side effects at every visit (and about 4 weeks after starting or changing the dose): ask directly about restlessness and do a short movement check; use a formal rating scale at least once a year (more often if high risk)

Screening at every visit for tardive dyskinesia — involuntary movements that can last — with a formal check at least yearly (every 6 months if high risk): look early for small face, tongue or hand movements
Fall risk and blood pressure lying and standing at every visit early on and after dose changes; advice to change position slowly
Weight/BMI at baseline, around 8 and 12 weeks after start or dose change, then quarterly; consider waist circumference at baseline and annually
Fasting plasma glucose/A1C around 4 months after initiation, then annually (more often if abnormal or high risk)
Lipid panel around 4 months after initiation, then annually (more often if abnormal or high risk)
Blood count (CBC) when needed; checked more closely if your white-cell count was low to begin with or a medicine has lowered it before

Blood salts, kidney and liver tests yearly (or sooner if needed); sodium watched closely in older adults because antipsychotics as a group can cause low blood sodium (hyponatremia), which can cause confusion, headache or seizures
Prolactin: ask about symptoms at every visit until the dose is stable; check the level if there are symptoms (sexual problems, period changes, milky nipple discharge, breast growth in men)
Temperature regulation counseling during heat exposure and strenuous exercise: hydration and warning signs of heat illness

special_populations.pregnancy: Data for second-generation antipsychotics as a group do not show a clear overall increase in major birth defects, but data for lurasidone itself are limited. Antipsychotics taken in the last three months of pregnancy can cause movement symptoms and/or withdrawal in the newborn (agitation, abnormal muscle tone, feeding problems, breathing trouble, sleepiness, shaking). Avoiding relapse is often the priority—stopping a medicine that works can raise the risk of relapse. The lowest dose that works is used, avoiding multiple medicines when possible, with symptoms tracked using a validated tool throughout pregnancy.
special_populations.lactation: Lurasidone passes into breast milk. Limited data from one breastfeeding mother suggest low exposure for the baby (relative infant dose reported <1%) and no side effects seen in that case, but evidence is thin. If breastfeeding during treatment, watch the baby for sleepiness, poor feeding, irritability, unusual movements and slowed development—especially if the baby is premature or low birth weight, or if other sedating medicines are involved. The lowest dose that works is used, avoiding multiple sedating medicines when possible.
special_populations.pediatric: Bipolar depression: approved on its own down to age 10. Schizophrenia: approved in teenagers. Children and teenagers may have a higher risk of movement side effects and need careful checks of weight/BMI, blood sugar/A1C and cholesterol, plus movement checks. Whether it is still helping long term should be reviewed regularly as part of a whole treatment plan (therapy, school supports, family work).
special_populations.geriatric: Antipsychotics should be avoided for behavior problems linked to dementia or delirium unless non-medicine approaches have failed and the person is at risk of harming themselves or others. Antipsychotics raise the risk of death in dementia-related psychosis. If used for appropriate conditions (eg, schizophrenia or bipolar disorder), the lower range of adult doses is used, raised slowly, with checks for dizziness on standing, falls, movement symptoms, thinking and sodium.
special_populations.renal_impairment: CrCl <50 mL/min: start 20 mg daily; max 80 mg/day. CrCl ≥50 mL/min: no adjustment.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Moderate hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh B): start 20 mg daily; max 80 mg/day. Severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh C): start 20 mg daily; max 40 mg/day.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Increased in fed state; taking with ≥350 calories increases exposure substantially compared with fasting
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Primarily hepatic via CYP3A4; has active and inactive metabolites
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Requires food (≥350 calories) for reliable absorption; grapefruit may increase serum concentrations

dosing.titration: Latuda is typically taken once daily in the evening with food (at least 350 calories). The food requirement is not optional—without it, absorption drops hard. Dosing depends on the psychiatric indication and special factors like kidney/liver function and age.

discontinuation.taper_guidance: With chronic psychiatric illness, switching is often safer than “just stopping,” especially if Latuda is controlling psychosis or bipolar depression. If stopping is the plan, taper gradually over weeks to months so you can catch early relapse signals and reduce withdrawal reactions (agitation, anxiety, insomnia, sweating, GI upset, tremor, dyskinesias). If discontinuation is due to a serious adverse effect, the plan may need to be faster—this is where specialist guidance matters.

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Latuda (lurasidone) is used to treat {link:condition:schizophrenia:schizophrenia} and {link:condition:bipolar-depression:bipolar depression} (depressive episodes in bipolar I disorder). In psychiatry, it’s a go-to when you want antipsychotic benefits with a generally more weight-friendly profile than many alternatives—while still respecting the trade-offs like akathisia, parkinsonism, and rare but serious reactions.
items: {link:condition:schizophrenia:Schizophrenia}: Helps reduce hallucinations, delusions, disorganization, and agitation over time
{link:condition:bipolar-depression:Bipolar I depression}: Treats the depressive phase (not acute mania/hypomania)
Adjunct option (adults): Can be combined with lithium or divalproex for bipolar depression
off_label: Bipolar depressive episodes with mixed features
Major depressive disorder with mixed features

sections.heading: What People Feel

quotes: It didn’t flip a switch, but the heaviness started loosening after the first week.
I noticed I could get out of bed without negotiating with my brain for an hour.
Less despair. More ability to function.

items.category: Thinking feels less noisy (schizophrenia spectrum symptoms)
quotes: My mind felt less chaotic. Not perfect—just quieter.
The edges of paranoia softened over a couple weeks.
I felt more anchored in reality.
My body wanted to pace even when my mind wanted to rest.
It wasn’t anxiety exactly—it was like my legs had their own agenda.
I felt restless in my skin after dose increases.
items.note: Akathisia is one of the most common deal-breakers. It often shows up early or after titration.

quotes: It made me sleepy at night, which honestly helped.
I got wired at bedtime and couldn’t settle.
My sleep was choppy for the first couple weeks.
items.note: Evening dosing can help some people tolerate side effects, but not everyone.

quotes: When I took it without food, it felt like I took nothing.
With a real meal, it worked better—and I stopped getting random nausea.
I had to build it into my routine or I’d forget the food part.
items.note: Food isn’t optional with Latuda. Absorption drops a lot without it.

sections.intro: Everyone’s response is personal, but here’s what tends to show up in real life—especially in the first few weeks:

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Latuda isn’t an instant tranquilizer. It’s more of a steady-build medication—early changes first, then deeper improvement over weeks.
key_points: Within 1 week (often): early improvement in bipolar depression can start showing up
1–2 weeks: early schizophrenia symptom shifts may begin (less intensity, less agitation)
4–6 weeks: fuller effect is more likely to be noticeable and consistent
Once daily dosing: long half-life supports daily dosing rather than multiple times per day
Food is part of the dose: taking it with ≥350 calories meaningfully changes how much medication your body absorbs

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Latuda can be effective for bipolar depression and schizophrenia, but it typically works in layers: early shifts in the first 1–2 weeks, followed by steadier improvement over 4–6 weeks. Consistency matters—and with this medication, the food requirement is part of consistency.
sections.clinical_details: In practice, response is strongly tied to (1) taking it with sufficient food and (2) tolerability during titration, especially around akathisia and parkinsonism. If someone ‘fails’ Latuda while taking it fasting, that may not be a real trial. If someone can’t tolerate akathisia, efficacy becomes irrelevant—management and switching strategies matter.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Not approved for dementia-related psychosis. Antipsychotics raise the risk of death in older adults with dementia-related psychosis.
sections.black_box: Older adults with dementia-related psychosis who are treated with antipsychotic medicines have a higher risk of death. Lurasidone is not approved for treating dementia-related psychosis.
other: Suicidal thoughts/behaviors: In short-term studies, antidepressants increased this risk in children, teenagers and young adults; watch for worsening mood or new suicidal thoughts and tell your prescriber right away (this warning is usually included when the medicine is used for mood).
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS): rare but life-threatening—fever, rigidity, confusion, autonomic instability
Tardive dyskinesia: risk rises with time and total exposure; can be persistent
Metabolic changes: weight, glucose, and lipids can change even if risk is lower than some other antipsychotics
Orthostatic hypotension/syncope and falls: especially early, with dose changes, or in older adults
Seizure risk: use caution in people with a seizure history or lowered seizure threshold
Temperature dysregulation: higher risk during heat exposure, dehydration, strenuous exercise
patient_counseling: Take Latuda with at least 350 calories every time. If you skip the food, you may be under-dosing without realizing it.
Call urgently for high fever + muscle stiffness + confusion (possible NMS).
Report restlessness you can’t control (akathisia), new tremor/stiffness, or swallowing problems—these can be movement side effects that need fast fixes.
Stand up slowly and hydrate, especially early on—dizziness and fainting can happen.
If you’re older or medically fragile, fall risk is real. Build in safety (night lights, slow position changes).
Tell your clinician about all meds and supplements—CYP3A4 interactions can make levels spike or crash.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most common psychiatric-relevant issues: akathisia (restlessness), extrapyramidal symptoms (parkinsonism), drowsiness or insomnia, agitation/anxiety, and nausea. Metabolic risk is usually lower than many antipsychotics, but not zero.
plain_language_list: Drowsiness or feeling sedated (more common at higher doses, often improves)
Agitation/anxiety or feeling keyed up (can overlap with akathisia)
Prolactin-related effects (sexual side effects, menstrual changes, breast symptoms)

serious: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS): fever, severe rigidity, confusion, autonomic instability. MEDICAL EMERGENCY.
Tardive dyskinesia: involuntary movements (face/tongue/limbs), risk increases with long-term exposure and age; can be persistent.
Severe orthostatic hypotension/syncope and falls: injury risk, especially in older adults or dehydration.
Hematologic abnormalities: leukopenia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, anemia—monitor CBC if history of low counts or symptoms of infection.

Cardiac conduction issues/QT prolongation: overall QTc effect is minimal compared with many antipsychotics, but postmarketing QT prolongation has been reported—use caution with cardiac risk factors or interacting meds.
Temperature dysregulation/heat stroke risk: especially during heat exposure, dehydration, strenuous exercise.
Suicidal ideation reported postmarketing: monitor mood and safety, especially during early treatment or changes.

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions

items.with: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (eg, ketoconazole, clarithromycin, ritonavir, voriconazole, mibefradil)
items.risk: Marked increase in lurasidone exposure → higher risk of EPS, sedation, hypotension, and other toxicity
items.action: Contraindicated. Choose a different antipsychotic or a non-interacting anti-infective/antiviral strategy.

items.with: Strong CYP3A4 inducers (eg, rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St. John's wort, avasimibe)
items.risk: Marked decrease in lurasidone levels → loss of efficacy, relapse risk
items.action: Contraindicated. Avoid combination; use an alternative agent.

items.action: Avoid grapefruit products while taking Latuda.

items.with: Other CNS-active meds that worsen movement side effects (certain antidepressants, stimulants, other antipsychotics)
items.risk: Higher risk of akathisia/parkinsonism/EPS through additive dopamine blockade or activation effects
items.action: Use caution with polypharmacy; monitor EPS closely during changes.

items.with: Blood pressure-lowering meds or dehydration states
items.risk: Orthostatic hypotension and syncope risk increases
items.action: Hydration, slow position changes, and close monitoring during initiation/titration.

sections.intro: Latuda is primarily metabolized by CYP3A4. Strong inhibitors can raise levels dangerously, and strong inducers can make it stop working. This is one of the most important interaction profiles to respect.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: With chronic psychiatric illness, switching is often safer than “just stopping,” especially if Latuda is controlling psychosis or bipolar depression. If stopping is the plan, taper gradually over weeks to months so you can catch early relapse signals and reduce withdrawal reactions (agitation, anxiety, insomnia, sweating, GI upset, tremor, dyskinesias). If discontinuation is due to a serious adverse effect, the plan may need to be faster—this is where specialist guidance matters.
key_points: Don’t stop abruptly unless there’s a serious adverse effect requiring urgent discontinuation.
Taper over several weeks to months when possible to reduce withdrawal symptoms and detect symptom recurrence early.

Withdrawal symptoms can include agitation, anxiety, insomnia, sweating, GI symptoms, chills/warmth waves, tremor, restlessness, dizziness/vertigo, dyskinesias, and return of psychosis or mood symptoms.

If switching antipsychotics: common strategies include cross-titration, overlap-and-taper, or (less commonly) abrupt change with careful monitoring; relapse risk level should drive how conservative you are.
If schizophrenia relapse risk is high, clinicians may overlap (keep the current med stable while the new med reaches a therapeutic dose) before tapering the first medication.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Latuda is typically taken once daily in the evening with food (at least 350 calories). The food requirement is not optional—without it, absorption drops hard. Dosing depends on the psychiatric indication and special factors like kidney/liver function and age.

adult.schizophrenia_initial: 40 mg PO once daily in the evening within 30 minutes of food (≥350 calories); consider 20 mg once daily for first-episode psychosis or sensitivity to side effects
adult.schizophrenia_titration: Increase in 40 mg increments no sooner than every 3 days based on response and tolerability; monitor akathisia, parkinsonism, and sedation during titration
adult.schizophrenia_typical: 40 to 80 mg/day; use the lowest effective maintenance dose
adult.bipolar_depression_initial: 20 mg PO once daily in the evening within 30 minutes of food (≥350 calories)
adult.bipolar_depression_titration: Increase by 20 mg increments every ≥2 days based on response and tolerability
adult.mdd_mixed_features_initial: 20 mg PO once daily in the evening within 30 minutes of food (≥350 calories) for 7 days
adult.mdd_mixed_features_titration: After day 7, increase by 20 mg every 2 to 7 days based on response and tolerability
adult.postpartum_psychosis_initial: 40 mg PO once daily in the evening within 30 minutes of food (≥350 calories)
adult.postpartum_psychosis_titration: After 3 days increase to 80 mg once daily; after 2 to 3 additional days may increase further up to 160 mg/day over ~1 week based on response and tolerability
adult.renal_impairment: CrCl <50 mL/min: Start 20 mg PO daily; maximum 80 mg/day (CrCl ≥50 mL/min: no adjustment)
adult.hepatic_impairment: Child-Pugh B: Start 20 mg PO daily; maximum 80 mg/day. Child-Pugh C: Start 20 mg PO daily; maximum 40 mg/day (Child-Pugh A: no adjustment)
adult.older_adults: Use lower-end adult doses and titrate slowly; avoid for dementia-related behavioral symptoms unless nonpharmacologic strategies fail and there is risk of harm; monitor falls, orthostasis, sodium, and movement symptoms closely

sections.simple_explanation: Latuda is usually once daily. The single most important dosing rule is food: take it with at least 350 calories or you won’t absorb enough. Dose increases should be slow enough to catch akathisia, stiffness, sedation, or blood pressure drops early. Kidney and liver impairment lower your safe maximum dose.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Pregnancy and postpartum are high-stakes contexts where the risk of untreated illness can be huge, and medication decisions should be shared and specialist-guided. For older adults, antipsychotics carry higher risks (falls, stroke, cognitive effects, and higher mortality in dementia-related psychosis). For kids and teens, metabolic and movement monitoring matters even if a medication is considered “lower risk.”
sections.pregnancy: Class-level data for second-generation antipsychotics do not show a clear major increase in congenital malformations overall, but lurasidone-specific data are limited. Third-trimester exposure to antipsychotics can lead to newborn EPS and/or withdrawal symptoms (agitation, abnormal tone, feeding issues, respiratory distress, somnolence, tremor). Avoiding relapse is often the priority—stopping an effective medication can raise relapse risk. Use the lowest effective dose and avoid polytherapy when possible; monitor symptom severity with a validated tool throughout pregnancy.
sections.lactation: Lurasidone is present in human milk. Limited data from one lactating patient suggest low infant exposure (relative infant dose reported <1%) and no observed adverse events in that case, but evidence is thin. If breastfeeding during treatment, monitor the infant for sedation, poor feeding, irritability, motor abnormalities, and slowed development—especially if the infant is premature/low birth weight or if other sedating medications are involved. Use the lowest effective dose and avoid multiple sedating meds when possible.
sections.pediatrics: Bipolar depression: approved down to age 10 (on its own). Schizophrenia: approved in adolescents. Children and teenagers may have higher EPS risk and need careful metabolic monitoring (weight/BMI, glucose/A1C, lipids) and movement monitoring. Long-term usefulness should be reviewed regularly as part of a total treatment plan (therapy, school supports, family work).
sections.geriatrics: Avoid antipsychotics for behavioral problems associated with dementia or delirium unless non-medicine approaches fail and the person is at risk of harming themselves or others. Antipsychotics increase the risk of death in dementia-related psychosis. If used for appropriate conditions (eg, schizophrenia or bipolar disorder), use the lower range of adult dosing, titrate slowly, and monitor orthostasis, falls, movement symptoms, cognition and sodium.
sections.hepatic: Moderate hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh B): start 20 mg daily; max 80 mg/day. Severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh C): start 20 mg daily; max 40 mg/day.
sections.renal: CrCl <50 mL/min: start 20 mg daily; max 80 mg/day. CrCl ≥50 mL/min: no adjustment.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Adherence and dosing-with-food check at every visit: confirm ≥350 calories each dose and consistent timing
Mental status and target symptoms every visit: mood, psychosis intensity, agitation, sleep, functioning

Akathisia/EPS every visit (and ~4 weeks after initiation or dose change): ask directly about restlessness and do a brief movement exam; use a formal rating scale at least annually (more often if high risk)
Tardive dyskinesia screening every visit and formally at least annually (every 6 months if high risk): look for subtle face/tongue/hand movements early
Fall risk and orthostatic vitals every visit early on and after dose changes; counsel on slow position changes
Weight/BMI at baseline, around 8 and 12 weeks after start or dose change, then quarterly; consider waist circumference at baseline and annually
Fasting plasma glucose/A1C around 4 months after initiation, then annually (more often if abnormal or high risk)
Lipid panel around 4 months after initiation, then annually (more often if abnormal or high risk)
CBC as clinically indicated; monitor more closely if low baseline WBC/ANC or history of drug-induced leukopenia/neutropenia
Electrolytes/renal/liver function annually (or sooner if clinically indicated); monitor sodium closely in older adults due to SIADH/hyponatremia risk class-wide
Prolactin: ask about symptoms at every visit until dose is stable; check level if symptoms (sexual dysfunction, menstrual changes, galactorrhea, gynecomastia)
Temperature regulation counseling during heat exposure and strenuous exercise: hydration and warning signs of heat illness

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Latuda is an oral tablet. Generics are available in the same strengths. Tablets should be taken with food and are generally not recommended to be split, crushed, or cut (the effects of altering tablets haven’t been fully evaluated).
items: Tablets: 20 mg, 40 mg, 60 mg, 80 mg, 120 mg (brand and generic availability varies by country)
Administration: Once daily with food (≥350 calories), ideally at the same time each day

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Latuda works by balancing dopamine and serotonin signaling in the brain—mainly by blocking dopamine D2 receptors and serotonin 5-HT2A receptors, with additional activity at 5-HT7 and partial agonism at 5-HT1A. The dopamine piece targets psychosis and agitation; the serotonin profile may help mood and cognition. It has little to no meaningful activity at histamine H1 or muscarinic M1 receptors, which is one reason it’s often less sedating and less anticholinergic than some alternatives—though side effects can still happen.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Latuda is a common choice when treating schizophrenia or bipolar depression, especially if weight gain, diabetes risk, or lipid issues are a major concern with other antipsychotics. It’s not a medication for acute mania/hypomania. The biggest practical rule is absorption: you need a real meal (≥350 calories). If you don’t build that into your routine, you can end up with inconsistent benefit and confusing side effects. Titration should be guided by tolerability—akathisia and parkinsonism are the side effects that most often determine whether Latuda is the right fit.

faqs.a: Latuda (lurasidone) is used to treat schizophrenia and depressive episodes in bipolar I disorder (bipolar depression). It’s not a treatment for acute bipolar mania or hypomania.

Some people notice early changes within about 1–2 weeks (sometimes sooner for bipolar depression), but the more consistent benefit usually builds over 4–6 weeks. If you’re not taking it with enough food, it can look like it “isn’t working” even when the dose is right on paper.

faqs.q: Do I really have to take Latuda with food?
faqs.a: Yes. Latuda needs at least 350 calories to absorb properly. Without food, your body gets way less of the medication—so you can end up with inconsistent results and a very confusing trial.

faqs.q: What’s the most common reason people stop Latuda?
faqs.a: A strong inner restlessness (akathisia) is a big one. It can feel like anxiety but it’s more physical—pacing, can’t sit still, “crawling” energy. The good news: it’s often manageable if caught early, and sometimes it means raising the dose more slowly or choosing a different medication.

Compared with many antipsychotics, Latuda is usually associated with minimal to low weight and metabolic risk. But “lower risk” doesn’t mean “no risk.” Some people still gain weight or have changes in glucose or lipids, so monitoring matters.

faqs.q: What medications can’t be taken with Latuda?
faqs.a: Medicines that strongly slow or strongly speed up how lurasidone is broken down are the main problem, and generally should not be used with it (they can make levels dangerously high or make the medicine stop working). Grapefruit can also raise levels—avoid it.

faqs.q: Is Latuda approved for dementia-related psychosis?
faqs.a: No. Antipsychotics raise the risk of death in older adults with dementia-related psychosis, and Latuda is not approved for that use.

faqs.q: How do I stop Latuda safely?
faqs.a: Don’t stop suddenly unless there’s a serious side effect that requires stopping right away. If stopping is the plan, lower the dose gradually over weeks to months so you can catch early relapse symptoms and reduce withdrawal reactions like agitation, anxiety, trouble sleeping, sweating, shaking, stomach upset, and return of psychosis or mood symptoms.

Latuda has been used off-label in postpartum psychosis in some specialist-guided protocols. Postpartum decisions are high-stakes—treatment should be individualized, and risks of untreated illness are real. If breastfeeding, infant monitoring for sedation/feeding issues is important because lurasidone can be present in milk.

faqs.q: What should be monitored while taking Latuda?
faqs.a: At visits: symptoms, side effects, movement symptoms (restlessness, stiffness, involuntary movements), blood pressure when standing and fall risk, and whether you’re taking it as prescribed—including with food. Over time: weight/BMI, blood sugar/A1C, cholesterol and prolactin symptoms. Blood counts and other blood tests are checked when needed, especially if there’s a history of low white blood cells or other risk factors.
